slides.title: Chapter 10: The Bitcoin Network
slides.sub: How nodes find each other, pass blocks and payments, and what moved since print

items.body: Picture: the Bitcoin logo, public domain (Wikimedia Commons). Python 3.14.6; Bitcoin Core 31.1 results are recorded, not run here.

slides.notes: This deck explains how the Bitcoin network works: who is on it, how nodes find each other, and how blocks and payments travel. Every number on a result picture was read from one recorded run of Bitcoin Core 31.1 on a test chain, or computed with the chapter's own Python library.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.sub: Three parts; every number is a slide you can jump to

items.label: code examples with a picture of each result

slides.notes: The route has three parts that follow the order of the chapter. Five true stories and twenty-two code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every listing here can be run and edited there.
slides.take: Three parts, twenty-two examples, five true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

items: Who is on the network, and what does a node say when it first meets another?
How does a new node find its first peers, and how many links does it keep?
How can a block travel in a few hundred bytes, and why does speed matter?
Where does a payment wait, and what happens to one that arrives before its parent?
How can a phone check a payment without the chain?
What did Bloom filters leak, and how do block filters turn the question around?
What does the encrypted transport hide, and what does it leave open?

slides.notes: The seven questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter.

slides.notes: The Bitcoin network is a crowd of ordinary computers that follow the same rules. This part shows who they are, what a node says when it first meets another, and which services it offers.

slides.title: Network: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: The Network
items.meaning: The computers that follow the same rules and pass the same messages.
items.analogy: Think of a road system that no single company owns.

items.label: Bitcoin
items.meaning: A money system and a network, run by software that anyone may run.
items.analogy: Think of an open recipe book that every kitchen cooks from.

items.label: peer-to-peer networks, Bitcoin as
items.meaning: Every participant is both client and server, and nobody is in charge.
items.analogy: Think of a village market with no manager.

items.label: Bitcoin network
items.meaning: The nodes that speak the Bitcoin protocol to each other over TCP.
items.analogy: Think of a club whose members all speak one dialect.

items.label: Node Types and Roles
items.meaning: Nodes differ in what they store and what they do for others.
items.analogy: Think of a town where some keep the archive and others a diary.

items.label: nodes
items.meaning: A node is a computer that runs Bitcoin software and joins the network.
items.analogy: Think of a post office in a national postal system.

slides.title: The handshake: version, then verack
slides.sub: Two nodes greet each other before anything else

groups.note: The recorded greeting between two test nodes running Bitcoin Core 31.1.

rows: seq = [c for t, c, n in e['sequence']]
groups.note: The messages arrive in a fixed order, version first.

rows: hello = tuple(v[x] for x in k)
groups.note: The version message names the software, the protocol and the chain height.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: the greeting of two nodes
The first four messages are version, wtxidrelay, sendaddrv2 and verack.

slides.notes: Two nodes cannot trade blocks until they have greeted each other. The first message is version, naming the software, the protocol and the chain height, and verack confirms it. This greeting was recorded from Bitcoin Core 31.1 on a test chain. It is example 1 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A node speaks first with version; verack accepts it

slides.title: A message is a 24-byte frame
slides.sub: Magic, command, length and checksum come before any payload

groups.note: A verack message has no payload at all, so only the frame remains.
Four fields make the frame: network magic, command, length and checksum.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: the 24 bytes of a verack
The main-network magic is f9beb4d9. Four fields, 24 bytes, and no payload.

slides.notes: Every message starts with the same 24 bytes. The magic tells which network it belongs to, the command names the message, the length says how much follows, and the checksum guards the payload. Verack has no payload at all. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Even an empty message has a frame of 24 bytes

items.analogy: Think of an auditor who rechecks every receipt in person.

items.label: archival full nodes
items.meaning: A full node that keeps every block since the first.
items.analogy: Think of a library that never throws a book away.

items.label: peers
items.meaning: The other nodes that one node is directly connected to.
items.analogy: Think of the neighbours you can call without a go-between.

items.label: Bitcoin Core
items.meaning: The reference software, written by volunteers, that most nodes run.
items.analogy: Think of the standard edition of the recipe book, with many editors.

items.label: mining
items.meaning: The work of finding new blocks; miners also run nodes.
items.analogy: Think of a lottery whose winner writes the next page of the ledger.

slides.title: Services: what a node offers
slides.sub: A bit field in the greeting names the services of a node

groups.note: Two nodes of the run, a full node and a pruned node, list their services.

rows: gone = [s for s in full if s not in pruned]
groups.note: The pruned node has dropped the NETWORK flag: it keeps only recent blocks.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: services in the greeting
Only the pruned node leaves out NETWORK: it has deleted old blocks.

slides.notes: Services travel as bits in the greeting. A full node offers NETWORK, meaning it can serve the whole chain, while a pruned node has deleted old blocks and leaves that bit out. Both are recorded from the same run. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A pruned node drops the NETWORK flag but keeps relaying what it has

slides.sub: Like a postal service without a post office: letters pass from hand to hand.

slides.title: Peers and blocks: key concepts (1 of 4)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Network Discovery
items.meaning: A new node finds its first peers, then learns about many more.
items.analogy: Think of a newcomer who asks the phone directory, then friends.

items.label: DNS seeds
items.meaning: Servers that answer a DNS query with addresses of reachable nodes.
items.analogy: Think of a phone directory that hands out a few numbers.

items.label: blocks
items.meaning: A block bundles transactions and names the block before it.
items.analogy: Think of a ledger page that cites the page before it.

items.label: blockchain
items.meaning: The chain of all blocks, each committing to the hash of its parent.
items.analogy: Think of a ledger whose pages are glued, so none can be swapped.

items.label: syncing blockchain
items.meaning: A new node downloads headers first, then the blocks, and checks them.
items.analogy: Think of reading the contents page before asking for chapters.

items.label: UTXOs (unspent transaction outputs)
items.meaning: The outputs not yet spent; a full node keeps this set to check payments.
items.analogy: Think of the coins in the drawer, not those already handed over.

slides.notes: These cards cover 6 key concepts of the part Peers, blocks and transactions. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 10.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: DNS seeds hand out addresses
slides.sub: The first contact of a node that knows nobody

groups.note: The node asked eight DNS seeds for addresses and counted the IPv4 answers.
Each seed answered with twenty to thirty addresses; the default port is 8333.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: IPv4 addresses per DNS seed
8 seeds answered with 20 to 29 addresses each; the default port is 8333.

slides.notes: A new node has no peers, so it asks the DNS seeds that are written into its code. Each seed answered with a different list of reachable nodes. The node then dials them on the default port, 8333, and learns more from there. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Eight seeds gave twenty to thirty IPv4 addresses each, for one default port

slides.title: addr against addrv2
slides.sub: How nodes tell each other about other nodes

groups.note: Two peers asked for addresses, one with the old addr and one with addrv2.
A reply never holds more than 23 percent of the address book.
addrv2 adds a network id and variable length, so Tor and I2P fit.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: two address messages
Network id 1 is IPv4 and 2 is IPv6; longer ids carry Tor and I2P addresses.

slides.notes: Nodes gossip addresses to each other. The old addr message has room for IPv4 and IPv6 only, while addrv2 gives each address a network id and a length, so longer onion and I2P addresses fit. A reply is capped at a share of the address book. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: addrv2 can carry Tor and I2P addresses; the old addr could not

slides.title: Connection types and their limits
slides.sub: Not every link relays everything

groups.note: The node opened three kinds of links, each recorded with what it relays.
Bitcoin Core keeps eight full-relay links and two block-relay-only links.
At most 125 links in all, counting those that call in.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: links of one node (Tx: payments, Addr: addresses)
Limits in the source: 8 full-relay, 2 block-relay-only, 125 links in all.

slides.notes: A node keeps different kinds of links. Full-relay links carry everything, while block-relay-only links carry blocks but no payments and no addresses, which makes them harder to spy on. The limits are constants in the source, read from the saved file. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Block-relay-only links carry no payments and no addresses

slides.title: Eight connections, one liar
slides.sub: A node is only as honest as the peers it happens to meet

items.cap: Total solar eclipse - NASA / Aubrey Gemignani, public domain, Commons

items: WHAT: On 12 August 2015, at USENIX Security in Washington, Ethan Heilman and colleagues presented Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin's Peer-to-Peer Network.
WHY: An attacker who controls every connection of a victim can feed it a false world and use it for double spending.
HOW: The attacker needs enough IP addresses to fill the victim's connection slots; the authors measured the cost by simulation and on live nodes.
SO WHAT: Bitcoin Core now keeps anchor connections and two block-relay-only links, and picks peers from different autonomous systems.

items.body: Stand-in picture: an eclipse, not the paper.

items.who: Ethan Heilman and Alison Kendler of Boston University, Aviv Zohar of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and Sharon Goldberg of Boston University
items.where: the 24th USENIX Security Symposium in Washington, D.C., 12 to 14 August 2015

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2015-08-12. At the USENIX Security Symposium in Washington, D.C., which began on 12 August 2015, Ethan Heilman, Alison Kendler, Aviv Zohar and Sharon Goldberg presented Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin's Peer-to-Peer Network. The lesson is that a node is only as honest as the peers it happens to meet.

slides.title: Headers first: 80 bytes a block
slides.sub: How a new node syncs the chain

groups.note: A new node first asks a peer for headers, not for blocks.
One reply holds at most 2000 headers; the second reply held 101.
A header has a fixed size, so the whole chain of headers is small.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: headers fetched by a new node
Each header is 80 bytes; the whole chain of 2,101 headers took two replies.

slides.notes: A new node asks for headers before blocks. Each header is 80 bytes and a reply holds up to 2000, so in this run two replies carried the whole chain of 2101 headers. The node checks they link up, then downloads the blocks. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Two thousand headers per reply; the whole chain of headers is small

slides.title: Peers and blocks: key concepts (2 of 4)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: transactions
items.meaning: Payments that peers announce, fetch and forward before a miner takes them.
items.analogy: Think of letters passed from hand to hand toward a postbox.

items.label: unconfirmed transactions
items.meaning: Valid transactions that no block contains yet.
items.analogy: Think of cheques handed in but not yet cleared.

items.label: Mempools and Orphan Pools
items.meaning: Each node keeps its own waiting areas for transactions.
items.analogy: Think of a shop with a waiting list and a shelf of incomplete orders.

items.label: memory pool
items.meaning: The valid, unconfirmed transactions that one node holds.
items.analogy: Think of each shop's own waiting list.

items.label: orphan pools
items.meaning: Transactions whose parent is unknown wait here until it arrives.
items.analogy: Think of a child's form that waits for the parent's signature.

slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Relay by wtxid and the fee filter
slides.sub: How a payment is announced to a peer

groups.note: The node announced two transactions, one cheap and one dear.
A peer that sets a fee filter hears only of the dearer one.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: who is told of which payment
A filter of 5,000 sat/kvB is 5 sat/vB: the cheaper payment is not announced.

slides.notes: A node announces a payment by its witness id, not by the plain id. A peer can also say that it wants only payments above a fee rate. In the run, the peer with a filter heard of the dearer payment only. It is example 8 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A fee filter keeps cheap payments away from a peer that does not want them

slides.title: An orphan waits for its parent
slides.sub: A payment that arrives before the one it spends

groups.note: A child transaction is sent before its parent, so the node cannot take it.
The node asks the sender for the missing parent.

rows: late = tuple(o[x] for x in k)
groups.note: Once the parent arrives, both sit in the memory pool.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: the order of events
The child is kept aside, not dropped; its parent releases it.

slides.notes: A child payment can arrive before the payment it spends. The node cannot check it yet, so it keeps it aside and asks the sender for the parent. When the parent arrives, both enter the memory pool. It is example 9 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The node asks the sender for the parent instead of dropping the child

slides.title: Every node has its own memory pool
slides.sub: The waiting list is local; the chain state is shared

groups.note: Node F holds six unconfirmed transactions; node G, never told, holds none.
Yet both agree on the set of unspent outputs.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: payments waiting in two nodes
Both nodes hold the same 107 unspent outputs: the chain state agrees.

slides.notes: A memory pool holds payments that are valid but not yet in a block, and each node has its own. In the run one node held six and the other none, yet the set of unspent outputs, which only blocks change, was identical on both. It is example 10 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Pools may differ between nodes, yet the unspent outputs agree

slides.title: Peers and blocks: key concepts (3 of 4)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Compact Block Relay
items.meaning: A block is sent as short ids of transactions the peer already has.
items.analogy: Think of telling a friend the page numbers of a book they own.

items.label: low-bandwidth mode (compact block relay)
items.meaning: The peer announces the block and sends the compact block on request.
items.analogy: Think of a waiter who asks before bringing the dish.

items.label: high-bandwidth mode (compact block relay)
items.meaning: The peer pushes the compact block at once, before full checks.
items.analogy: Think of a courier who runs over with the parcel unasked.

items.label: block-finding races
items.meaning: Two miners may find a block almost together; speed decides which stays.
items.analogy: Think of two runners finishing within a breath.

items.label: Private Block Relay Networks
items.meaning: Miners pass blocks to each other over fast private networks.
items.analogy: Think of an express lane beside the public road.

slides.title: Compact blocks: 332 bytes, not 3,062
slides.sub: BIP 152 sends only what the peer lacks

groups.note: The test node sent one block of 13 transactions as a compact block.
Twelve short ids of 6 bytes stand for what the peer already holds.
Compare the bytes on the wire with the full block.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: bytes of one block of 13 payments
The compact block is 10.8 percent of the size: 12 short ids of 6 bytes, the coinbase sent whole.

slides.notes: A peer already knows most payments of a new block from its memory pool. So the block travels as a header, a short id of 6 bytes per payment, and the few payments the peer cannot have. The saving here is about nine tenths. It is example 11 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The peer rebuilds the block from its own memory pool

slides.title: Sending a block as a list of short codes
slides.sub: Do not resend what the receiver already knows

items.cap: Optical fibre strands - BigRiz, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: On 27 April 2016 BIP 152, Compact Block Relay, was assigned to Matt Corallo; Suhas Daftuar wrote the Bitcoin Core code.
WHY: A node already knows most payments of a new block from its memory pool, so sending them again wastes time.
HOW: The block travels as a header, a 6-byte short id per payment and the few payments the peer cannot have, such as the coinbase.
SO WHAT: In this chapter's run, a block of 13 payments went out as 332 bytes instead of 3,062.

items.body: Stand-in picture: optical fibre, not the BIP.

items.who: Matt Corallo, a Bitcoin Core and relay-network developer, and Suhas Daftuar, who wrote the Bitcoin Core implementation
items.where: the bitcoin/bips repository on GitHub, and Bitcoin Core 0.13.0, released in August 2016

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2016-04-27. On 27 April 2016 the number 152 was assigned to the BIP Compact Block Relay by Matt Corallo. The lesson is that do not resend what the receiver already knows.

slides.title: Two ways to announce a compact block
slides.sub: BIP 152 lets each peer choose its mode

left.head: Low-bandwidth mode
rows: The peer first announces the block.
We ask for the compact block if we want it.
Like a waiter who asks before bringing the dish.

right.head: High-bandwidth mode
rows: The peer sends the compact block at once.
It does so before it has fully checked the block.
Like a courier who runs over with the parcel unasked.

slides.notes: A peer may announce first and wait to be asked, or push the compact block unasked. Pushing saves one round trip, which matters when blocks race. Announcing first wastes nothing on a peer that already has the block.
slides.take: Pushing saves a round trip; announcing first saves bandwidth

slides.title: The block-finding race
slides.sub: Why a slow block risks a rival

groups.note: Blocks arrive on average every 600 seconds, at random moments.
The chance that a rival block appears while yours still travels.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: chance of a rival block, percent, by delay
A block that takes 60 seconds to travel has a 9.5 percent chance of a rival.

slides.notes: Blocks arrive at random, on average every ten minutes, so while your block is still travelling someone else may find one. The longer the delay, the likelier the rival, which is why fast relay matters most to miners. It is example 12 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A block that travels for a minute has about a one in ten chance of a rival

slides.title: Peers and blocks: key concepts (4 of 4)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: private block relay
items.meaning: Blocks pass over a dedicated, fast channel, not the open network.
items.analogy: Think of a private courier for urgent parcels.

items.label: FEC (Forward Error Correction)
items.meaning: Extra parity data lets a receiver rebuild lost packets without asking.
items.analogy: Think of a spare part packed in the box, so no repair call is needed.

items.label: Bitcoin Relay Network
items.meaning: Matt Corallo's relay network for miners, built to move blocks quickly.
items.analogy: Think of a ring road built only for lorries.

slides.title: A parity part rebuilds a lost part
slides.sub: The idea behind forward error correction

rows: parts = [b'compac', b't bloc', b'k mess', b'age!!!']
groups.note: Cut a message into four parts and add one parity part, their XOR.
Lose any one part; the parity and the other three rebuild it.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: four parts and one parity part
The message is whole again: compact block message!!!.

slides.notes: Forward error correction sends a little extra so that losses can be repaired without asking again. The simplest form is one parity part: the XOR of all others. XOR the survivors with the parity and the lost part appears. It is example 13 in the chapter code tab of the course page.

slides.sub: Nakamoto's calculation for an attacker with a share q

slides.notes: An attacker tries to build a longer secret chain. Nakamoto computed the chance of ever catching up from z blocks behind. With ten percent of the hash rate it falls quickly; with thirty percent it stays large for longer. It is example 15 in the chapter code tab of the course page.

Both patterns are found (yes); 6 of 16 bits are set, so strangers sometimes pass.

slides.notes: A Bloom filter sets a few bits for each item added, and a test looks at the same bits. If one is clear, the item was definitely not added; if all are set, it may have been. slides.title: The filter that told on the wallet
slides.sub: A privacy tool can leak more than it hides

items.cap: Bloom filter diagram - David Eppstein, public domain, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: BIP 37 was assigned to Mike Hearn and Matt Corallo on 24 October 2012: light clients send a Bloom filter of their addresses to a node.
WHY: In 2014 Arthur Gervais and colleagues at ETH Zurich showed that this leaks considerable information about the addresses of the user.
HOW: BIP 111 added the service bit NODE_BLOOM in 2015, and Bitcoin Core 0.19.0.1 turned the service off by default.
SO WHAT: In this chapter's run, a default node closed the connection of a peer that sent filterload.

items.who: Mike Hearn and Matt Corallo, who wrote BIP 37, and Arthur Gervais, Srdjan Capkun, Ghassan Karame and Damian Gruber of ETH Zurich, who tested it
items.where: the bitcoin/bips repository, the ETH Zurich security group, and Bitcoin Core 0.19, which turned the service off by default in 2019
items.linkText: Gervais et al.: Bloom filter privacy (paper)

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2012-10-24. BIP 37 was assigned to Mike Hearn and Matt Corallo on 24 October 2012: a light client would send a Bloom filter of its addresses to a full node and receive only matching transactions. The lesson is that a privacy tool can leak more than it hides.

slides.title: Golomb coding sends differences
slides.sub: The trick behind compact block filters

groups.note: Sort the numbers, send the first, then only the differences.
Differences need fewer bits than the numbers themselves: 8 instead of 10.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: the five numbers (orange) and their differences (slate)
The largest number needs 10 bits, the largest difference 8. Adding back restores the list: yes.

slides.notes: A block filter is a sorted list of hash values. Instead of sending each value, send the first and then only the gaps between neighbours. The gaps are smaller than the numbers, so each needs fewer bits. It is example 18 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Sorted numbers differ by less than they are, so differences take fewer bits

slides.title: Golomb-Rice coding is lossless
slides.sub: Unary quotient plus a few remainder bits

groups.note: Each difference is written as a unary quotient and p remainder bits.
Decoding returns the original list exactly, and the bits are fewer.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: bits for five numbers
Decoding returns the same five numbers, and the coded set is smaller than the fixed width.

slides.notes: Golomb-Rice coding writes each gap as a quotient in unary followed by p remainder bits. It is lossless: decoding returns the identical list. Here it needs fewer bits than a fixed width, and for a real filter the saving is larger. It is example 19 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Decoding gives back the exact list, in fewer bits

slides.title: An anonymous post turned the filter around
slides.sub: Reverse the question and the leak disappears

items.cap: Solomon W. Golomb - National Science Foundation, public domain, Commons

items: WHAT: On 9 May 2016 a developer writing as bfd posted Committed Bloom filters to the bitcoin-dev mailing list.
WHY: A Bloom filter makes the client reveal its addresses; the idea was to turn the question around.
HOW: The full node builds one small filter per block; the client downloads it and tests its own addresses privately.
SO WHAT: Olaoluwa Osuntokun and Alex Akselrod wrote BIP 157 and 158 with Golomb-coded sets, and our code reproduced all ten vectors.

items.body: Stand-in picture: Solomon Golomb, whose coding the filter uses.

items.who: an anonymous developer who wrote as bfd, and Olaoluwa Osuntokun and Alex Akselrod, who wrote BIP 157 and 158
items.where: the bitcoin-dev mailing list, and the Lightning Labs project Neutrino

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2016-05-09. On Monday 9 May 2016 a developer writing as bfd posted to the bitcoin-dev list the message Committed Bloom filters for improved wallet performance and SPV security. The lesson is that reverse the question and the leak disappears.

slides.title: Transport v1 shows its magic, v2 hides it
slides.sub: What an eavesdropper can see on the wire

groups.note: The same two nodes spoke the old transport once and the new one once.
Can an eavesdropper see the network magic or the word version?
The v2 stream looks like random bytes: near 8 bits of entropy per byte.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, P, R and src are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: what an eavesdropper sees
Random data would give 8 bits per byte; the v2 stream gives 7.953.

slides.notes: In the old transport the network magic and the word version are plain to see. In version 2 neither appears, and the stream has almost eight bits of entropy per byte, which is what random data looks like. It is encrypted, not authenticated. It is example 21 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Version 2 traffic looks like random bytes

slides.title: From a closed proposal to the default
slides.sub: Defaults decide how private a network is

items.cap: Enigma machine - Rama, CC BY-SA 2.0 FR, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: On 8 March 2019 BIP 324, the v2 encrypted transport, was assigned to Dhruv Mehta, Tim Ruffing, Jonas Schnelli and Pieter Wuille.
WHY: Version 1 sends everything in the clear, so anyone on the path can read it and tell Bitcoin traffic from other traffic.
HOW: Bitcoin Core 26.0 added v2 as an option and 27.0 made it the default; it encrypts but does not authenticate.
SO WHAT: In this chapter's run, the v2 stream showed neither the magic bytes nor the word version.

items.body: Stand-in picture: an Enigma machine, not BIP 324.

items.who: Dhruv Mehta, Tim Ruffing, Jonas Schnelli and Pieter Wuille, the authors of BIP 324; Jonas Schnelli had written the earlier BIP 151
items.where: the bitcoin/bips repository, and the releases Bitcoin Core 26.0 (December 2023) and 27.0 (April 2024)

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2019-03-08. Jonas Schnelli proposed encrypting peer connections in BIP 151 on 23 March 2016, a proposal that drew mixed comments and was closed with a replacement named. The lesson is that defaults decide how private a network is.

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.sub: One line per group of slides, each provable from its slides

items: Nodes greet each other with version and verack, in a 24-byte frame, and announce their services.
A new node finds peers by DNS seeds and addr, and keeps eight full-relay and two block-relay-only links.
Headers come first; compact blocks send about a tenth of a block; each node keeps its own memory pool.
A light client checks a Merkle path; Bloom filters leaked addresses, so block filters turn the question around.
Version 2 encrypts peer traffic but does not authenticate it; Tor and I2P hide who is who.

slides.notes: These five lines are the deck in miniature. A line that feels unproven should send you back to its code slide, because every figure in it was read from the recorded run or computed there. The chapter code tab of the course page reruns all twenty-two examples.
slides.take: If a line feels unproven, the code slide of its part carries the receipt
